name: Religions trivia (medium)
description: 50 medium questions about the world's religions, large and small: beliefs, practices, holidays, history; respectful, no claims about which is true. Written by Claude from cited web pages; every question names its page. Checked by a second model pass; the questions it flagged were corrected or left out.

source.name: Web pages cited on each question

items.question: Which Sikh Guru commanded Khalsa Sikhs in 1699 to wear the Five Ks at all times?
items.explain: Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru, established the Khalsa in 1699 and commanded its members to wear the Five Ks.

items.question: In Sikhism, what is the kara, one of the Five Ks worn by initiated Sikhs?
items.explain: The kara is the steel (or iron) bracelet. The other Ks are kesh (uncut hair), kangha (comb), kachera (undergarment) and kirpan (sword).

items.question: Sikhs observe Diwali to commemorate the release from Mughal imprisonment of which Guru?
items.explain: Sikhs mark Diwali as the time Guru Hargobind was freed after being imprisoned by the Mughal emperor Jahangir.

items.question: In Buddhism, the Noble Eightfold Path corresponds to which of the Four Noble Truths?
answers: The path leading to the end of suffering
items.correct: The path leading to the end of suffering
items.explain: The Eightfold Path is identified with the fourth Noble Truth, the way that leads to the cessation of suffering.

items.question: In Buddhist symbolism, what do the eight spokes of the dharma wheel (dharmachakra) represent?
answers: The elements of the Noble Eightfold Path
The great disciples of the Buddha
The stages of rebirth in samsara
The vows taken by Buddhist monks
items.correct: The elements of the Noble Eightfold Path
items.explain: The Noble Eightfold Path is often shown as the dharma wheel, with each of its eight spokes standing for one element of the path.

items.question: Which of the following is one of the eight factors of the Buddhist Noble Eightfold Path?
items.explain: The eight factors are right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration. Worship, sacrifice and devotion are not among them.

source.title: The Noble Eightfold Path: The Way to the End of Suffering

items.question: In Islam, what is the name of the Pillar that consists of fasting during the month of Ramadan?
items.explain: Sawm is fasting during Ramadan, the fourth of the Five Pillars of Islam.

items.question: Which Pillar of Islam involves paying alms to benefit the poor and needy?
items.explain: Zakat is the obligatory giving of alms for the benefit of the poor and needy, one of the Five Pillars of Islam.

items.question: The Muslim pilgrimage known as the hajj takes place in which month of the Islamic calendar?
items.explain: The hajj rites take place from the 7th to the 12th day of Dhu al-Hijjah, the last month of the Islamic year.

items.question: What must every Muslim recite at least once in a lifetime, aloud and with understanding, as the first of the Five Pillars?
answers: The shahadah, the profession of faith
The adhan, the call to prayer
The Fatiha, the Quran's opening chapter
items.correct: The shahadah, the profession of faith
items.explain: The shahadah declares that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is God's Prophet. Every Muslim must recite it at least once in a lifetime.

items.question: Jains regard Mahavira as which in a succession of Jinas (Conquerors)?
items.explain: Jains hold that their religion was revealed in stages by a series of Conquerors, of whom Mahavira was the 24th.

items.question: What is the Sanskrit name for the central Jain doctrine of noninjury to all living beings?
items.explain: Ahimsa means noninjury and is the standard by which all actions are judged in Jainism.

items.question: Which idea does Jainism reject, according to Britannica?
answers: A creator god who made the world
Karma as a force binding the soul
items.correct: A creator god who made the world
items.explain: Jainism has no belief in a creator god, though it teaches karma, rebirth and liberation (moksha).

items.question: How many great vows (mahavratas) of renunciation did Mahavira teach, one more than his predecessor Parshvanatha had preached?
items.explain: Mahavira taught five great vows, whereas Parshvanatha had preached only four.

items.question: After years of intense fasting and meditation, Vardhamana became known as Mahavira. What does this title mean?
items.explain: Vardhamana was called Mahavira, meaning "Great Hero," after more than 12 years of fasting and meditation led to enlightenment.

items.question: In Japan, what does a torii gate at the entrance of a Shinto shrine mark?
answers: The boundary between ordinary space and the shrine's sacred ground
The burial ground of the shrine's founder
The route of the annual festival procession
The entrance to the priests' living quarters
items.correct: The boundary between ordinary space and the shrine's sacred ground
items.explain: A torii is a symbolic gateway, often painted red, that separates the ordinary world from the sacred precincts where the kami reside.

items.question: In Shinto custom, what is the purpose of the Shichi-go-san festival held on November 15?
answers: Children of certain ages visit a shrine to give thanks and pray for growth
Families burn old charms at the shrine to mark the new year
Newlyweds pronounce their first vows before the shrine's kami
Fishermen carry the shrine's sacred symbol through the harbor
items.correct: Children of certain ages visit a shrine to give thanks and pray for growth
items.explain: Shichi-go-san (Seven-Five-Three) is when boys of five and girls of three and seven visit a shrine to thank the kami for protection and pray for healthy growth.

items.question: Which Japanese island is home to a Shinto shrine best known for its "floating" torii?
items.explain: Itsukushima Shrine on Itsukushima island, popularly called Miyajima, is famous for its torii that appears to float in the water.

items.question: A traditional Japanese house has a Shinto altar and a Buddhist altar. Whom does the Buddhist altar honor?
items.explain: The Shinto altar is for the household's tutelary kami and Amaterasu Omikami, while the Buddhist altar is for the family ancestors.

items.question: What is the principal holy text of Zoroastrianism?
items.explain: The major beliefs of Zoroastrianism are found in the Avesta, its principal holy text.

items.question: Ahura Mazdā, the supreme god of Zoroastrianism, has a name meaning what?
items.explain: The Avestan name Ahura Mazdā means "Wise Lord."

items.question: Which Persian king, who reigned from 522 to 486 BCE, worshipped Ahura Mazdā as the greatest of all gods?
items.explain: Darius I and his successors worshipped Ahura Mazdā as the greatest of gods and protector of the just king.

items.question: In Zoroastrian belief, what is the name of the Destructive Spirit who opposes Ahura Mazdā?
items.explain: The Avesta describes Ahura Mazdā in a primeval battle against Angra Mainyu, the Destructive Spirit.

items.question: The name Bahá'u'lláh, taken by the founder of the Bahá'í Faith, means what in Arabic?
items.explain: Mírzá Ḥosayn ʿAlí Núrí became known as Bahá'u'lláh, which means "Glory of God" in Arabic.

items.question: The title "the Báb," given to the forerunner of Bahá'u'lláh, means what in Arabic?
items.explain: Mírzā ʿAlī Moḥammad of Shīrāz was known as the Báb (Arabic "Gateway"), and his movement led to the Bahá'í Faith.

items.question: Where is the Baháʼí World Centre, a site Baháʼu'lláh identified as the future resting place of the Báb?
items.explain: In 1891 Baháʼu'lláh pointed to a spot on Mount Carmel in Haifa as the Báb's resting place, which became the site of the Baháʼí World Centre.

source.title: Factsheet: The Baháʼí faith - Religion Media Centre

items.question: In which year was the Bábí faith, the movement from which the Baháʼí Faith grew, founded in Iran?
items.explain: The Báb founded the Bábí faith in Iran in 1844, and the Baháʼí religion grew out of it.

items.question: The name Rastafari comes from the pre-coronation title and name, Ras Tafari, of which Ethiopian ruler?
items.explain: Ras Tafari Makonnen was crowned in 1930 as Haile Selassie I, whom Rastas regard as central to their faith.

items.question: In Rastafari practice, what are "bingis"?
items.explain: Britannica lists "bingis" among Rastafari rituals, alongside prayer services and ganja smoking for "itation" (meditation).

items.question: The name of the Hindu festival Diwali comes from the Sanskrit word dipavali, meaning what?
items.explain: Dipavali means "row of lights," which is why Diwali is called the Festival of Lights.

source.title: Why Diwali Is Called the Festival of Lights

items.question: In North India, Diwali celebrates which deity's return to the city of Ayodhya after defeating the demon king Ravana?
items.explain: In Northern India, Diwali honors Rama's return to Ayodhya after his victory over Ravana. In South India it is tied to Krishna's defeat of Narakasura.

source.title: Why Diwali Is Called the Festival of Lights

items.question: The Upanishads, the philosophical texts that end the Vedas, take their name from a term that traditionally meant what?
items.explain: Upanishad traditionally meant "sitting near a teacher," though it was originally understood as "connection" or "equivalence."

items.question: In Hindu thought, the goal of moksha (literally "release") is freedom from what?
answers: The cycle of death and rebirth
items.correct: The cycle of death and rebirth
items.explain: Moksha means release from samsara, the cycle of death and rebirth.

items.question: On which date of the Hebrew calendar does Passover begin?
items.explain: Passover takes place in early spring, beginning on the 15th of the Hebrew month of Nisan.

items.question: What does the matzah eaten at the Passover seder symbolize?
answers: The hurried departure of the Israelites from Egypt
The wheat harvest celebrated at Shavuot
The Temple sacrifice of the Paschal lamb
The manna that fell in the wilderness
items.correct: The hurried departure of the Israelites from Egypt
items.explain: Matzah is unleavened bread that recalls how the Israelites left Egypt in such a hurry that their bread had no time to rise.

items.question: The Hebrew word seder, the name of the Passover ritual meal, literally means what?
items.explain: Seder is Hebrew for "order," reflecting the set sequence of steps in the Passover meal.

items.question: The afikoman, a piece of matzah at the Passover seder, takes its name from a Greek word meaning what?
items.explain: Afikoman comes from a Greek word for "dessert," and matzah is the official dessert of the seder meal.

items.question: Which mountain is the holiest site of the Samaritans, where they perform their Passover sacrifices?
items.explain: Samaritans still sacrifice a sheep at Passover on Mount Gerizim, their holiest site.

items.question: Which Roman emperor convened the First Council of Nicaea in 325?
items.explain: Emperor Constantine convened the council, the first ecumenical council of the Christian church, to resolve the controversy over Arianism.

items.question: The First Council of Nicaea condemned which doctrine, which held that Christ was a created being and not fully divine?
items.explain: The council condemned Arius and the Arian heresy, and affirmed the equality of God the Father and God the Son.

items.question: The ancient city of Nicaea, site of the first ecumenical council of the Christian church, is now which Turkish town?
items.explain: Ancient Nicaea is today the town of İznik in Turkey.

items.question: According to tradition, Martin Luther nailed his Ninety-five Theses to the door of a church in which German town?
items.explain: Tradition says Luther posted the theses on the Castle Church door in Wittenberg on October 31, 1517, though historians dispute whether this happened.

items.question: In what year did the Eastern and Western branches of Christianity split, well before the Protestant Reformation?
items.explain: Britannica notes that the Eastern and Western branches of Christianity had already split in 1054, long before Luther's Reformation.

items.question: In 1520, which pope demanded that Martin Luther recant statements from his writings?
items.explain: Pope Leo X demanded that Luther recant. Luther publicly burned the papal bull threatening excommunication and was then excommunicated.

items.question: Luther's Ninety-five Theses responded to the selling of indulgences to pay for rebuilding which church in Rome?
items.explain: The theses were written in response to indulgences being sold to fund the rebuilding of St. Peter's Basilica.

items.question: Which figure, who flourished in the 6th century BCE, is traditionally regarded as the founder of Daoism and author of the Daodejing?
items.explain: Laozi is traditionally regarded as the founder of Daoism and author of its classic, though scholars think the Daodejing had several authors.

source.title: Origin and general characteristics of Daoism

items.question: In Daoist philosophy, what does the concept of wuwei mean?
answers: Nonaction, acting in harmony with nature
items.correct: Nonaction, acting in harmony with nature
items.explain: Wuwei literally means "no action," the practice of taking no action that is not in accord with the natural course of the universe.

items.question: Which thinker, known as "Master Zhuang," lived in the 4th–3rd century BCE and was a major interpreter of Daoism?
items.explain: Zhuangzi (Zhuang Zhou), who lived from 369 to 286 BCE, was a major interpreter of Daoism, and the book bearing his name is a Daoist classic.

items.question: Malak Ṭāʾūs, the chief divine being of the Yazidi religion, is known in English by what name?
items.explain: Malak Ṭāʾūs means "Peacock Angel," and Yazidis worship this chief divine being in the form of a peacock.

items.question: Where is the tomb of Sheikh Adi, located at the holiest temple of the Yazidi religion?
items.explain: Lalish, in Iraq's Nineveh Plains, is the Yazidis' holiest temple and the site of Sheikh Adi's tomb.
